doc.title: Karl Berger interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, August 11, 2014

title: More musicians than ever, and New York's costs
summary: Berger finds hope in the growing Improvisers Orchestra and young players, and contrasts cheap lofts earlier with costs now in New York.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Yeah. So I feel that the respect for music is like completely deteriorated from that point of view you know. But the refreshing thing that I’m seeing, and I don’t know where that’s going to lead, is the more difficult it gets to be a musician, the more musicians there are. It’s like literally thousands and thousands of kids who just don’t want to do anything else but play music, which is like very refreshing to see but it also there is an element of desperation that the rest of the world doesn’t seem to offer all that much so people go there because there is really some kind of spiritual reward at least you know. And so I mean the Improvisers Orchestra has like 60 or 70 players who call me who want to play. And I thought I could do it like three or four times and then it would dissipate. It’s growing. And the quality of the music is like skyrocketing. It’s like amazing. So there is such a level of music out — so I’m thinking there will eventually be some kind of qualitative jump of some sort. It will happen. I don’t know exactly how that’s going to be and whether we’re going to be around to see it. But we really had to like adapt you know, to a whole other situation over the last 20, 30 years. We had a huge change.
Well I appreciate that sort of bright note you ended on about your Improvisers Orchestra. Maybe things will —

Yeah that is like so refreshing to see that, that like so many kids, not just kids, as I’m saying, some performers are in their 60’s and 70’s and 80’s, are out here to play. Don’t © Fillius Jazz Archive -20-

forget also that a city like New York, which is probably the only city in the world that has such an abundance of musicians in one place, has completely different conditions because when we were starting out in New York we would live in lofts and, for like a couple of hundred dollars or less, and could play all day. And now everybody lives in little cubicles and have to come up with $2000 a month or more, and fights to play in six or seven different bands of which they get a maximum of like one rehearsal per gig of no more than two hours because three hours would be too expensive you know. It’s like crazy. People cannot play together anymore. But the pressure is getting more and more. And I think it will come to a boil eventually. Something will happen. And my feeling is there’s a lot of creative energy out there.
And something really interesting is going to happen.
